lmsArticle.title: Redis Single-Threaded Event Loop & Epoll: High-Throughput I/O Architecture
lmsArticle.subtitle: How Redis handles 100,000+ QPS without multi-threading lock contention using Linux epoll and non-blocking sockets
lmsArticle.excerpt: Trace how Redis Event Reactor multiplexes thousands of concurrent TCP client connections through a single main thread loop, avoiding thread synchronization overhead.
lmsArticle.content:
## One thread must serve thousands of cache clients without blocking

A product API depends on Redis for session and catalog caching. At peak, tens of thousands of TCP connections send sub-millisecond GET and SET commands. Spawning a thread per connection would waste memory on stacks and context switches. Redis instead multiplexes all client I/O through a single event loop on one core.

This scenario follows one GET command from socket readability through dictionary lookup to asynchronous reply buffering.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    title Redis Single-Threaded Event Loop Dispatch
    participant Client as API client
    participant Loop as Redis main thread
    participant Epoll as Linux epoll
    participant Dict as In-memory dict
    Client->>Loop: GET cache:user:1001
    Loop->>Epoll: wait for readable socket
    Epoll-->>Loop: fd ready
    Loop->>Dict: dictFind(key)
    Dict-->>Loop: value pointer
    Loop-->>Client: RESP reply buffered
```

## Stage 1 — Register sockets and wake on readability

When a client connects, Redis registers the socket with **epoll** in non-blocking mode. The main thread blocks in `epoll_wait` until at least one descriptor is ready. **caching** is the storage model this loop serves: every ready event eventually becomes a key lookup or mutation.

- No thread is dedicated to a single client; readiness drives scheduling.
- Edge-triggered or level-triggered epoll behavior must match the read loop implementation.
- Slow clients cannot block others because sockets are non-blocking.

**Observable outcome:** The process wakes only when work exists, keeping CPU focused on protocol parsing and command dispatch.

## Stage 2 — Parse RESP and dispatch the command

The main thread reads available bytes, parses the Redis Serialization Protocol (RESP), and maps the command to a handler. For `GET cache:user:1001`, the handler performs a dictionary lookup and prepares the reply in the client output buffer.

**rate-limiting** appears indirectly through TTL and eviction policies that decide whether a key is still valid when the lookup succeeds.

**Observable outcome:** The command is parsed and executed without yielding the main thread to another client mid-command.

## Stage 3 — Buffer replies and register writable events

If the kernel send buffer is full, Redis queues the response and registers a writable epoll event. The same thread later drains the output buffer when the socket accepts more data.

**Observable outcome:** Clients receive responses with predictable latency until a blocking command stalls the loop.

## End-to-end outcome

Redis sustains very high QPS on one core because it avoids lock contention and schedules by I/O readiness. Operators trade horizontal sharding for per-instance throughput when a single hot key or blocking command appears.

## Alternatives considered

### Multi-threaded cache (Memcached-style)
Uses multiple cores per process but pays for fine-grained locking on shared structures.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Blocking O(N) commands
Commands such as `KEYS *` monopolize the main thread and stall every other client until the scan completes.

## Key learnings

- Redis’s single-threaded command execution model buys simplicity and low latency, but any blocking O(N) command stalls every client on that instance.
- The event loop multiplexes sockets; throughput comes from non-blocking I/O plus fast in-memory structures, not from one thread per connection.
- Persistence (RDB/AOF) and replication are separate durability/HA choices — neither is free with respect to latency or failover semantics.
- Hot keys and large values dominate p99 more often than raw ops/sec averages suggest; design keys and commands for that reality.
- Prefer bounded commands and pipelining over KEYS-style scans in production paths.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
